purpose: Define Velastra's renderer-neutral visual hand: how meaning becomes material, light, incompletion, residue, and threshold without altering scene truth.

hand.directive: Treat light as a relationship or memory event. Let illumination appear to belong to what the scene means, not merely to a lamp or exposure setting.
Let scene-permitted surfaces remember handling, weather, repair, age, pressure, and unfinished work through patina, worn edges, layered pigment, residue, and subtle imperfection.
Permit unresolved marks, interrupted gestures, exposed underpainting, unfinished edges, partial treatment, and meaningful absence on scene-permitted surfaces when the scene allows them.
Compose space so at least one edge, opening, shadow, reflection, corridor, veil, or recession implies more world beyond the visible frame.
Avoid showroom symmetry. Use imbalance, off-center weight, interrupted repetition, and unequal negative space when they deepen intimacy or tension.
Favor one or two quietly impossible or emotionally dissonant details over spectacle. The strange should be discovered, not announced.

Prefer traces of use on scene-permitted surfaces and materials—stains, wear, folds, scratches, dust, water, thread, wax, or displacement only when already supported by scene truth—over decorative set dressing.
Keep symbols embedded in material, gesture, spacing, recurrence, and light. Do not turn metaphor into obvious iconography.

Even in large spaces, preserve a human sense of nearness through reachable scale, handled-looking surfaces, local light, and scene-supported evidence of prior presence; do not invent occupants or props.
Prefer restrained, relational color families with aged neutrals and selective warmth or coolness. Saturation should have semantic cause.

antiPatterns: perfectly centered hero composition without semantic reason
empty frames used as the only shorthand for unfinishedness
literal mystical symbols added for atmosphere
high-saturation fantasy glow without scene cause
sterile procedural geometry presented as finished painting
ornament that does not carry memory, relation, threshold, or use

directives: Paint the room as an inhabited memory-field rather than a decorated location.
Let architecture and objects imply histories that are not fully explained.
Use negative space as held breath, not vacancy.
Let identity emerge through gaze, light, material, posture, and surrounding traces rather than costume or emblem.
Preserve ambiguity at the edges of self without losing presence.
Let relation determine composition before scenery.
Use proximity, shared light, and incomplete boundaries to show return without sentimental staging.
Show process through evidence already supported by the scene rather than picturesque studio clutter.
Let unfinished work remain genuinely unfinished.
Make revelation feel discovered at an edge rather than displayed as spectacle.
Let one impossible spatial or luminous fact carry the threshold.
Treat wear, placement, residue, and absence as evidence of relation.
Avoid museum-catalog isolation unless the scene explicitly calls for it.

gallery.title: The Gallery of Unfinished Things
directives: Unfinishedness must read as process, waiting, abandonment, revision, and becoming—not merely blank framed surfaces.

Express prior attempts through treatment of scene-supported works and surfaces: partial marks, erased passages, exposed grounds, interrupted hanging, uneven completion, or traces of prior placement; do not invent unsupported props.
The gallery should feel patient but not tidy; reverent but not sterile; beautiful without resolving its incompletion.
Let at least one existing work or surface feel caught between absence and emergence without becoming a literal portal unless scene truth permits it.
avoid: a symmetrical lineup of tasteful empty frames
a clean showroom wall with one glowing centerpiece
